notes.meaning: A person hears an official call in court to give evidence about a crime he knows about, but chooses to stay quiet. God warns that keeping silent when we should tell the truth makes us share in the wrongdoing. Followers of God are called to speak the truth plainly and help justice be done.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Some modern scholars understand this verse as hearing someone curse out loud in public, rather than a judge calling for witnesses in a court.

notes.meaning: A person accidentally touches the dead body of an unclean animal, like a wild beast or a rodent. Even if he did not realize it right away, he becomes ceremonially unclean, which means unfit to join in public worship, and is held guilty. God taught His people to pay close attention to purity in their everyday lives.

An Israelite might touch human uncleanness, such as a sick person or a diseased body, without noticing at first. As soon as he realizes what happened, he bears guilt for failing to follow the cleansing laws. God wants us to face our faults honestly as soon as they come to light.

A person makes a hasty vow out loud, promising to do something good or bad without thinking it through. Even if the promise was made carelessly, he is still guilty before God if he breaks it or swore to do something wrong. God expects us to use our words carefully and keep our word.

Anyone who becomes guilty of these offenses must openly admit the exact wrong he has done. Making an animal offering without admitting the fault would just be an empty ritual. True peace with God begins when we name our sins and turn away from them.

The person who sinned brings a female lamb or young goat to the priest as a sin offering. The priest then makes atonement, which means making things right between God and the sinner, so the person is forgiven. This animal dying in the sinner's place points forward to Jesus taking our punishment.

God provides an easier way for someone who is too poor to afford a lamb or goat. That person may bring two turtledoves or two young pigeons instead, one for a sin offering and the other for a burnt offering. The Lord shows that a person's lack of money will never block the way to His forgiveness.

The worshipper hands the two birds to the priest, who offers the sin offering first. The priest wrings the bird's neck from the back without cutting the head completely off. Sin had to be dealt with and forgiven before God would accept an offering of praise.

The priest splatters part of the bird's blood on the side of the altar and drains the rest at its base. Because this is a sin offering, the lifeblood of the bird is poured out before the Lord. This showed the worshipper how costly it is to remove the stain of sin.

The priest prepares the second bird as a burnt offering following the regular rules, and it is completely consumed by fire. Through these sacrifices, the priest makes atonement for the sinner, and God forgives the fault. The burnt offering showed that the forgiven person was now wholly dedicated to God again.

If a person is so poor that he cannot afford even two small birds, he may bring about two quarts of fine flour as a sin offering. He must not pour olive oil or frankincense on it, because it is an offering for sin rather than a joyful gift. God graciously makes a way for even the poorest person to find cleansing.

The poor worshipper gives the dry flour to the priest, who scoops up a handful of it. The priest burns that handful on the altar fire as a memorial portion, representing the whole gift given to the Lord. It stood as a sign that the sinner was turning back to God for mercy.

The priest burns the flour to make atonement for whichever sin the person committed, and the Lord grants full forgiveness. The rest of the flour is given to the priest for food, just like a regular grain offering. God shows that forgiveness does not depend on our wealth, but on His mercy.

The Lord speaks once again to Moses with a fresh set of instructions. This introduces rules for a new kind of sacrifice called the guilt offering. It shows that God cares deeply about how His people treat sacred things.

A person might accidentally misuse something dedicated to God, like eating holy food or forgetting to pay a tithe. When he learns of his error, he must bring a healthy ram valued at a set price in silver silver as a guilt offering. Even unintentional neglect of what belongs to the Lord is a serious matter.

The worshipper must repay the full value of the holy thing he harmed and add an extra twenty percent penalty. He pays this to the priest, who then offers the ram to make atonement so the sinner is forgiven. True repentance includes doing everything we can to make right the harm we caused.

A person might break one of the Lord's commandments without realizing it at the time. Even though he did not know he broke the law, he is still guilty and must bear responsibility for the wrong. We are accountable to God's standards even when we are not aware of our mistakes.

The person brings an unblemished ram of proper value to the priest as a guilt offering. The priest offers the ram to make atonement for the unintentional wrong, and God pardons the person. God provides a certain path to forgiveness for our hidden and forgotten faults.

God makes it clear that this ram is a true guilt offering because the person was truly guilty before the Lord. No sin can simply be ignored or forgotten without a sacrifice to make things right. God's perfect justice requires that every offense against Him be fully covered.
